options.C: Acute kidney failure
options.D: Severe muscle wasting

explanation: Stopping anti-seizure drugs suddenly can trigger a dangerous loop of continuous seizures called status epilepticus. Patient education on compliance is a major nursing duty! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h5)

question: Which type of fever stays consistently high all day with almost no drops?

options.A: Sustained fever
options.B: Remittent fever
options.C: Relapsing fever
options.D: Intermittent fever

explanation: You got it! A sustained fever stays high and steady without giving the patient much of a break throughout the day.

question: If a patient is given a new drug classed as an antihypertensive, what main effect should you expect?

options.A: Elevated blood glucose
options.B: Reduced joint inflammation
options.C: Increased bacterial cell death
options.D: Lowered blood pressure

explanation: Well done! 'Anti' means against, and 'hypertensive' refers to high blood pressure—so antihypertensives bring high blood pressure down.

question: Why do the kidneys often take a hit during prolonged body-wide asphyxia?

options.A: Lactic acid crystals block the small ureter tubes
options.B: They absorb too much carbon dioxide from the blood
options.C: They experience severe reduction in blood perfusion
options.D: The kidneys overproduce urine to flush out toxins

explanation: When the body runs low on oxygen, it goes into survival mode, pulling blood away from the kidneys and skin to protect the brain and heart. Sadly, this leaves the kidneys starved and vulnerable to damage.

question: What is the main job of the pudendal nerve in the external genitalia?

options.A: Regulating local skin temperature
options.B: Producing seminal fluid
options.C: Controlling testosterone synthesis
options.D: Providing somatic sensory feedback

explanation: The pudendal nerve acts as the messenger wire, carrying touch and pain signals from the genital skin back up to the brain.

question: What is the primary goal of the living will movement?

options.A: To give doctors full authority over end-of-life care
options.B: To speed up the legal probate process for families
options.C: To help patients control their medical treatment choices ahead of time
options.D: To reduce overall hospital costs for elderly patients

explanation: The entire movement centers on letting individuals make their treatment preferences known before they lose the ability to speak for themselves. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h1)

question: What is the primary objective of gathering psychosocial data in a hospital setting?

options.A: To force the client to change their personal lifestyle habits immediately
options.B: To shape safe, individual nursing care that addresses emotional and social needs
options.C: To prove that the client has no underlying mental health challenges
options.D: To reduce the amount of time nurses spend talking to family members

explanation: The information gathered helps nurses create care plans that treat the whole person, not just the physical disease. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T5#GNS222_U3_T5_h2)

question: A patient presents to the emergency ward with dry skin, a very high fever, blurry vision, and dilated pupils after taking an unknown medication. Which toxidrome is this?

options.A: Anticholinergic
options.B: Sympathomimetic
options.C: Cholinergic
options.D: Opioid

explanation: The classic presentation of dry skin, fever, confusion, and dilated pupils points directly to an anticholinergic poisoning syndrome. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T1#GNS215_U5_T1_h4)

question: Why do nurses constantly remind patients receiving radiation therapy not to wash off their skin treatment marks?

options.A: To prevent the patient from developing a severe skin allergy to the ink
options.B: To keep the hospital records accurate for billing and insurance purposes
options.C: To allow the radiation oncologists to track how fast the outer tumor is shrinking
options.D: To ensure precise daily alignment of the radiation beam to the exact tumor site

explanation: Spot on! Those little marks are like a bullseye. They make sure the radiation machine hits the exact tumor spot safely every single time.

question: What is the medical term for a smooth, red, and painful tongue linked to nutritional shortages?

options.A: Petechiae
options.B: Glossitis
options.C: Epistaxis
options.D: Jaundice

explanation: Glossitis just means inflammation of the tongue. It makes the tongue look smooth and red, and you'll often see it in patients with vitamin B12 or iron deficiencies.

question: Why is it so important to encourage a patient to drink lots of fluids after a bone scan?

options.A: To prevent severe dehydration caused by the strong magnetic fields
options.B: To replace the fluid lost during the mandatory fasting period before the test
options.C: To activate the chemical tracer so it can take clearer pictures of the spine
options.D: To help flush the remaining radioactive tracer out of the body through urine

explanation: Drinking plenty of water helps the kidneys wash out any leftover radioactive tracer quickly, lowering radiation exposure.

question: What is the single best way to prevent a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)?

options.A: Clamp the catheter for two hours every afternoon
options.B: Remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer medically necessary
options.C: Apply antibiotic ointment around the meatus three times a day
options.D: Disconnect the drainage tubing every morning to flush it out

explanation: You've got it! The golden rule of preventing catheter infections is taking the tube out the moment it's no longer needed.

question: How soon can a person's fertility return after an abortion procedure?

options.A: After exactly six months
options.B: Not for at least two years
options.C: As early as two weeks
options.D: Only after menopause begins

explanation: Surprise! Ovulation can bounce back in as little as two weeks. That's why talking about family planning early is so crucial before she leaves the clinic. [learn more](GNS226_U5_T007#GNS226_U5_T007_h5)

question: A patient wants to leave the ward early because they cannot afford their remaining hospital bill. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Connect the patient with the hospital social welfare unit or available support schemes
options.B: Threaten to call security if the patient attempts to leave the bed
options.C: Ignore the situation since financial matters are strictly administrative
options.D: Pay the hospital bill directly out of the nurse's personal salary

explanation: Well done! Hospital social workers are there to help bridge financial gaps and find workable payment solutions so patients can finish their care safely.

question: What is a major risk to a newborn if the mother receives strong pain opioids right before delivery?

options.A: Neonatal respiratory depression
options.B: Rapid premature bone growth
options.C: Severe congenital heart defects
options.D: Permanent hearing impairment

explanation: If opioids cross the placenta just before birth, the baby might be born a bit too sleepy to take a good first breath on their own.

question: After a patient has an upper endoscopy, what is the most important nursing check before giving them water?

options.A: Administering a large meal immediately to test stomach tolerance
options.B: Checking for active bowel sounds every fifteen minutes
options.C: Keeping the patient flat on their back for at least six hours
options.D: Confirming that the patient's gag reflex has returned before offering fluids

explanation: Spot on! The throat spray numbs the back of the throat, so we must wait for the gag reflex to come back to prevent them from choking on water.

question: A cancer patient says food smells too strong and tastes like metal. What is a helpful nursing tip?

options.A: Suggest serving foods cool or at room temperature to reduce strong smells
options.B: Tell the patient to force themselves to eat large portions anyway
options.C: Advise the patient to stop eating completely until treatment ends
options.D: Recommend adding extra iron supplements to every meal

explanation: Warm foods release strong vapors that trigger nausea. Serving meals cool helps hide those metallic tastes and smells. Clever nursing care!

question: A patient with a new forearm cast says the rough edge of the plaster is scratching their wrist. What should have been done with the stockinette to prevent this?

options.A: Stretching the stockinette tighter across the fingers
options.B: Soaking the outer stockinette in warm saline
options.C: Folding the stockinette edges back over the cast ends
options.D: Applying adhesive tape over the outer plaster

explanation: Rolling the extra stockinette material back over the edges of the hardened cast creates a smooth, protective border that stops skin irritation. You've got this!

question: A nurse is preparing to use a blood pressure cuff on a patient with unbroken skin. How should this item be classified and processed?

options.A: Semi-critical item requiring high-level chemical disinfection
options.B: Critical item requiring high-pressure steam sterilization
options.C: Non-critical item requiring low to intermediate-level disinfection
options.D: Sterile item requiring single-use disposal packaging

explanation: Blood pressure cuffs touch only intact skin, making them non-critical items that only need routine low or intermediate disinfection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a good reason to prescribe antibiotics along with draining an abscess?

options.A: The presence of severe surrounding skin redness and swelling
options.B: The patient developing a fever and systemic chills
options.C: The patient simply prefers taking pills over wound care
options.D: The patient having a compromised immune system

explanation: Antibiotics are powerful drugs reserved for spreading infections, fevers, or weak immune systems—never just because a patient prefers taking pills over doing proper wound care.

question: How does external radiation therapy primarily destroy cancer cells?

options.A: By using high-energy rays to damage cellular DNA and stop cell division
options.B: By lowering the patient's core body temperature to induce cellular death
options.C: By surgically removing the affected organ through a small skin incision
options.D: By flooding the circulatory system with cytotoxic chemical compounds

explanation: Well done! Radiation uses targeted high-energy beams to break the DNA inside cancer cells so they can't multiply anymore.

question: Why must nurses in local community clinics look beyond hospital walls when caring for patients?

options.A: Environmental and economic living conditions heavily impact health outcomes
options.B: Nurses are forbidden from providing care outside of enclosed rooms
options.C: Community members never visit hospitals for severe medical problems
options.D: Lab tests can only be accurately performed in outdoor market stalls

explanation: Understanding a patient's home and community environment helps explain why illnesses occur and how to prevent them. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h6)

question: Why is a single initial assessment insufficient for palliative care patients?

options.A: Palliative conditions and symptoms change rapidly over time
options.B: Patients usually forget their medical history on day one
options.C: Doctors prefer to change diagnoses daily without reason
options.D: Hospitals require a new paperwork form every single hour

explanation: Because disease trajectories fluctuate, ongoing re-assessment is necessary to catch new or worsening symptoms. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h2)

question: What usually triggers the body to develop secondary polycythaemia?

options.A: An autoimmune attack on bone marrow
options.B: An inherited defect in the platelets
options.C: Sudden heavy blood loss from injury
options.D: Chronic low oxygen levels in tissues

explanation: Spot on! When body tissues are short on oxygen over time, the body panics and pumps out more red blood cells to help.

question: What is the main danger of feeding a severely malnourished patient too quickly?

options.A: Sudden permanent loss of all digestive enzyme production
options.B: Immediate development of chronic kidney stone formation
options.C: Dangerous drops in key electrolytes like potassium and phosphate
options.D: Rapid hardening of the major arteries in the neck

explanation: Sudden food intake shifts electrolytes into cells too fast, which can shock the heart if we aren't careful. Slow and steady wins the race here!

question: What are two major health risks associated with early unprotected sexual intercourse in adolescents?

options.A: Sexually transmitted infections and unintended pregnancies
options.B: Chronic respiratory illness and severe joint pain
options.C: Nutritional deficiencies and bone density loss
options.D: Visual impairment and cardiovascular disease

explanation: Unprotected sexual contact exposes young people directly to pathogens causing infections and fails to prevent fertilization, leading to high rates of teenage pregnancy. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T9#GNS312_U3_T9_h1)

question: Why would a doctor order a diagnostic thoracentesis?

options.A: To measure how much oxygen the lungs can hold total
options.B: To find out the exact cause of a pleural fluid buildup
options.C: To prevent the development of a future heart attack
options.D: To permanently cure chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

explanation: Great thinking! When we take a little sample of that fluid to the lab, we can figure out why it started gathering in the chest in the first place.

question: What is a key instruction the nurse must give the patient before the procedure starts?

options.A: Take deep breaths continuously while the needle is in place
options.B: Remain as still as possible and avoid coughing during insertion
options.C: Stand up and walk around the room to help settle the fluid
options.D: Drink at least two liters of water right before the procedure

explanation: Sudden movements or coughs can cause the needle to scrape or puncture the delicate lung tissue. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T17#GNS221_U2_T17_h4)

question: Which factor is part of an environmental safety assessment for a client with balance problems?

options.A: Checking for loose rugs, poor lighting, and stairs
options.B: Checking the color of the paint on the bedroom walls
options.C: Counting the number of chairs in the living room
options.D: Measuring the room temperature and humidity levels

explanation: Environmental checks focus on removing physical hazards like tripping risks to prevent falls at home. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T5#GNS222_U3_T5_h7)

question: What common physical sensation do many patients report when experiencing a sudden heart dysrhythmia?

options.A: Muscle spasms
options.B: Abdominal cramps
options.C: Joint stiffness
options.D: Palpitations

explanation: Patients frequently feel palpitations, which they describe as a racing, skipping, or fluttering sensation in their chest. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T3#GNS213_U1_T3_h4)

question: Where does fertilization of the egg by the sperm normally take place in the female reproductive tract?

options.A: Ampulla
options.B: Isthmus
options.C: Cervix
options.D: Fimbriae

explanation: The ampulla is the wider middle section of the fallopian tube, providing just the right space for the sperm to meet and fertilize the egg.

question: A patient with sickle cell anaemia suddenly complains of a severe headache and trouble speaking. What is your priority nursing action?

options.A: Administer a mild oral pain reliever and reassess the patient in one hour
options.B: Perform a prompt neurological assessment and notify the primary provider immediately
options.C: Encourage the patient to drink two large glasses of cold water right away
options.D: Apply a warm compress to the forehead and turn off the overhead room lights

explanation: Trust your nursing instincts! Sudden neurological changes in a sickle cell patient can mean a stroke is happening. This is a medical emergency that needs immediate action.

question: Which cells make up the large majority of the outer layer of your skin (the epidermis)?

options.A: Melanocytes
options.B: Fibroblasts
options.C: Adipocytes
options.D: Keratinocytes

explanation: Keratinocytes are the most common cells in the epidermis! As they mature and move upward, they form a tough, protective shield for your body.

question: Which medication class is used long-term to lower uric acid production in the body?

options.A: Opioid analgesics like morphine
options.B: Xanthine oxidase inhibitors like allopurinol
options.C: Inhaled beta-agonists like albuterol
options.D: Loop diuretics like furosemide

explanation: Drugs like allopurinol block the enzyme that makes uric acid, helping keep future crystal build-up under control.

question: What is the primary goal of decision making in family planning?

options.A: Choosing pregnancy timing, spacing, and number of children
options.B: Ensuring every family has at least four children
options.C: Eliminating all future pregnancies for every household
options.D: Reducing overall healthcare spending in rural clinics

explanation: Family planning helps individuals and couples decide if, when, and how often to have children to protect their health and well-being. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T023#GNS226_U6_T023_h1)

question: A patient expresses deep regret over past actions and asks if God can ever forgive them. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Dismiss the worry because everyone makes mistakes
options.B: Tell the patient that nurses only handle physical medications
options.C: Advise the patient to stop thinking about the past
options.D: Acknowledge their concern and offer to connect them with a spiritual care provider

explanation: Spiritual distress is real pain. Acknowledging it and connecting them with a chaplain or spiritual leader gives them the holistic support they need.

question: When can palliative care be started for someone with a serious illness?

options.A: Only when the patient is discharged back home
options.B: Only during the final twenty-four hours of life
options.C: After all medical treatments have completely failed
options.D: Early in the disease course alongside curative treatments

explanation: Palliative care isn't just for the very end! It can start right from diagnosis, walking hand-in-hand with treatments meant to cure or manage the disease.

question: What shape does a single smooth muscle cell usually have?

options.A: Short, branched, and connected by intercalated discs
options.B: Spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus
options.C: Flat and square with rough borders
options.D: Long and cylindrical with multiple nuclei

explanation: Think of them like little tapered grains of rice—thicker in the middle and pointed at the ends, holding just one cozy nucleus right in the center.

question: Which of the following is NOT a blockage-related (post-testicular) cause of male infertility?

options.A: Blocked vas deferens
options.B: Congenital absence of the sperm ducts
options.C: Epididymal scarring from infection
options.D: Klinefelter syndrome

explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is a chromosomal condition affecting the testes, whereas the other options are physical blockages in the tubes that carry sperm.

question: Why is skin turgor checked over the clavicle or forearm during a physical assessment?

options.A: To evaluate the patient's overall hydration status
options.B: To measure the exact blood pressure in the upper body
options.C: To check for localized muscle weakness under the skin
options.D: To determine if the patient has a superficial fungal infection

explanation: Skin turgor reflects how quickly the skin returns to its normal flat position, which helps nurses estimate body fluid volume and hydration. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h1)

question: Which of the following is a major risk factor for puerperal sepsis?

options.A: Rapid spontaneous vaginal birth
options.B: Early ambulation after delivery
options.C: Exclusive breastfeeding
options.D: Prolonged rupture of membranes

explanation: When membranes rupture for a long time before delivery, bacteria have a direct open pathway to travel up into the uterus. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h3)

question: Why might a surgeon need to perform a craniectomy (removing a piece of the skull) after severe brain trauma?

options.A: To remove the primary injury site completely
options.B: To permanently cure the patient's concussion
options.C: To relieve dangerous pressure caused by brain swelling
options.D: To clean out surface dirt from a skull fracture

explanation: You got it! Taking off a piece of the skull gives a swollen brain room to expand outward instead of crushing vital areas inside.

question: How do many patients view healthcare workers when it comes to authority?

options.A: As temporary service providers who must follow orders
options.B: As individuals who frequently make intentional errors
options.C: As peers with identical medical training
options.D: As absolute authority figures whose judgment is unquestionable

explanation: Exactly! Culturally, many patients see healthcare providers as infallible experts, which makes them hesitant to speak up or ask questions.

question: Who is protected when a nurse properly uses isolation precautions?

options.A: Only the doctors working in the ward
options.B: Only the patient who is currently sick
options.C: Patients, healthcare workers, and visitors
options.D: Hospital management and administrators

explanation: Infection control keeps everyone in the hospital safe and sound—patients, your colleagues, and loved ones who come to visit!

question: What is the standard first-line injection used to treat uncomplicated gonorrhea?

options.A: Ceftriaxone
options.B: Penicillin G
options.C: Metronidazole
options.D: Vancomycin

explanation: Ceftriaxone as a single injection is our go-to treatment because older drugs unfortunately don't work well anymore due to resistance.

question: Which sign in an enlarged lymph node strongly points toward cancer (malignancy)?

options.A: Soft, tender, and mobile
options.B: Small, rubbery, and painful
options.C: Hard, fixed, and painless
options.D: Warm, pulsating, and soft

explanation: Cancerous lymph nodes are typically firm or hard, stuck tightly in place (fixed), and usually don't hurt when you press them.

question: Why does the biopsychosocial model work best for explaining drug addiction?

options.A: It focuses solely on the patient's current environmental stress
options.B: It looks at biological, psychological, and social factors together
options.C: It relies entirely on psychiatric medication history
options.D: It proves that genetics is the only true cause of drug use

explanation: Addiction is complex, and the biopsychosocial model acknowledges that body chemistry, mental health, and life surroundings all contribute. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T12#GNS125_U2_T12_h4)

question: What is the main goal of isolation tactics used in emotional abuse?

options.A: To help the victim save money by avoiding social gatherings
options.B: To encourage the victim to focus more on their personal career goals
options.C: To protect the victim from catching infectious community diseases
options.D: To increase the victim's dependence by cutting off their support systems

explanation: Abusers isolate victims from friends and family to make them completely dependent and reduce their chances of seeking help. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T9#GNS312_U4_T9_h3)

question: A patient's eyes and optic nerves are uninjured, yet they cannot make sense of what they look at. Which lobe should the nurse suspect is affected?

options.A: Occipital lobe
options.B: Frontal lobe
options.C: Parietal lobe
options.D: Temporal lobe

explanation: The eyes gather light, but the occipital lobe processes and interprets the actual images we see. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T23#GNS211_U3_T23_h5)

question: A patient uses crushed fresh leaves on a swollen joint. What kind of poultice is this?

options.A: An herbal poultice
options.B: A surgical poultice
options.C: A chemical poultice
options.D: A synthetic poultice

explanation: Using fresh plants or leaves directly falls under the category of traditional herbal poultices. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h3)

question: How do digital charts in an EMR help nurses keep an eye on vital signs?

options.A: By automatically discharging the patient when vitals normalize
options.B: By making it easier to spot trends and early signs of patient worsening
options.C: By replacing the need to manually measure blood pressure or pulse
options.D: By sending text messages directly to the patient's family members

explanation: Graphical charts lay out numbers over time so you can spot little changes before they turn into major emergencies. You've got this!

question: A mum mentions she is breastfeeding her baby but also giving thin porridge to help the baby sleep through the night. How do you assess this?

options.A: This is a healthy practice that ensures the infant stays full through the night
options.B: This technique prevents maternal exhaustion without affecting the infant
options.C: This practice is mixed feeding and increases the risk of HIV transmission
options.D: This method safely prepares the baby's stomach for solid foods early

explanation: Even though mums want better sleep, adding porridge early counts as mixed feeding and raises transmission risks. Gentle counseling here is key!

question: What is the main purpose of the evaluation step in the nursing process?

options.A: To write a formal medical diagnosis for the physician to sign
options.B: To calculate the total financial cost of hospital supplies used
options.C: To decide which nurse will work the night shift over the weekend
options.D: To determine whether established patient care goals have been successfully met

explanation: Evaluation is just checking our report card: did our nursing care help the patient reach their health goals?

question: Which vitamin is most commonly recommended as a first-line supplement for pregnancy nausea?

options.A: Vitamin D
options.B: Vitamin A
options.C: Vitamin C
options.D: Vitamin B6

explanation: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) is a safe, go-to supplement prescribed in antenatal clinics to help ease that queasy feeling.

question: Why is caring for someone with Pick's disease often so emotionally draining for families?

options.A: The disease progresses much faster than any other form of dementia.
options.B: Patients require constant surgical procedures throughout the illness.
options.C: Family members are legally required to pay for all hospital care.
options.D: The loss of personality and social filter can feel emotionally rejecting.

explanation: It hurts deeply when a loved one changes personality, loses their warmth, or acts out of character. Families need plenty of empathy and support from nurses to cope with this grief.

question: Why does bruising often show up a day or two after a sprain?

options.A: Infection has set into the joint capsule causing skin discoloration
options.B: The body is reacting negatively to the prescribed pain medication
options.C: Excessive synovial fluid is pushing pigments to the skin surface
options.D: Blood leaks from injured small blood vessels into the surrounding soft tissue

explanation: When tiny blood vessels tear during a sprain, the blood seeps out and slowly travels toward the surface of the skin, creating that classic bruise.

question: How do we classify used surgical blades and needles in the hospital?

options.A: General waste
options.B: Pathological waste
options.C: Sharps
options.D: Pharmaceutical waste

explanation: Great job! Any tool that can cut or puncture the skin, like needles and blades, is known specifically as a sharp.

question: How does passive faecal incontinence differ from urge incontinence?

options.A: It is caused strictly by eating spicy foods
options.B: The patient feels a strong urge but cannot hold it
options.C: Stool leaks out without any prior warning or sensation
options.D: It only happens during heavy physical exercise

explanation: Passive incontinence occurs silently because the patient lacks sensation and sphincter tone, whereas urge incontinence involves feeling the need to go but failing to reach the toilet in time. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a common feature of end-of-life care in Nigeria?

options.A: Involvement of extended family in medical discussions
options.B: Widespread legal use of formal living wills and advance directives
options.C: Strong influence of Christian and Islamic religious beliefs
options.D: Strict criminal prohibitions against assisted suicide and euthanasia

explanation: While family involvement, religion, and strict laws against euthanasia are very common in Nigeria, formal written living wills are still not widely used or legally integrated into everyday hospital practice yet.

question: Which of these is a great example of secondary data in a community assessment?

options.A: Focus group discussions with local market women
options.B: Direct visual observations of village water sources
options.C: Interviews conducted by nurses during home visits
options.D: Clinic registers and existing census reports

explanation: Spot on! Secondary data is information that was already collected by someone else and is sitting in existing records and reports.

question: What is the gold standard test to confirm a diagnosis of lymphoma?

options.A: Complete blood count
options.B: Excisional lymph node biopsy
options.C: Routine skin scraping
options.D: Fine-needle aspiration cytology

explanation: To be 100% sure, pathologists need to look at a whole lymph node under the microscope. Taking out the node (excisional biopsy) is the best way to do this.

question: Which complication involves dangerous pressure build-up inside an enclosed muscle compartment that cuts off blood supply?

options.A: Avascular necrosis
options.B: Fat embolism syndrome
options.C: Compartment syndrome
options.D: Osteomyelitis infection

explanation: Compartment syndrome occurs when swelling restricted by tight fascia compresses blood vessels and nerves, threatening limb survival. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T10#GNS222_U1_T10_h9)

question: What is the main reason developing countries experience more complications from unsafe injections?

options.A: A complete lack of trained nurses in regional clinics
options.B: Patients refusing oral medications in favor of injections
options.C: The natural resistance of tropical germs to standard soap
options.D: Supply shortages and poor waste management systems

explanation: Exactly. When clinics struggle with equipment shortages, it can unfortunately lead to dangerous workarounds like reusing syringes. You're building great clinical awareness! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h2)

question: When a drainage tube gets blocked, which of these actions is completely WRONG and dangerous?

options.A: Pushing a partially dislodged tube back into the body cavity
options.B: Checking the entire length of the tubing for accidental kinks
options.C: Inspecting the tube for visible blood clots or mucus plugs
options.D: Notifying the medical team if output remains absent

explanation: You got it! Pushing a slipped tube back inside drags surface bacteria straight into sterile tissues. Always check with your senior or doctor first.

question: Why do modern nurses view the stages of grief as flexible guidelines rather than strict rules?

options.A: Individuals move through grief stages in unpredictable ways, often skipping or repeating them
options.B: Patients only experience grief if they are told about the stages beforehand
options.C: The stages apply exclusively to children and never to adult patients
options.D: Theoretical models have been proven completely inaccurate through modern laboratory testing

explanation: You nailed it! Grief isn't a straight line. People heal at their own pace, often jumping back and forth between stages.

question: How can an expectant mother help her body absorb more iron from her food?

options.A: Consuming iron-rich foods along with vitamin C sources
options.B: Avoiding all fresh fruits and vegetables during meals
options.C: Drinking strong tea or coffee with every main meal
options.D: Taking her iron tablets exclusively on an empty stomach with milk

explanation: Vitamin C is iron's best friend! Taking iron with orange juice, tomatoes, or fresh fruits gives the gut a helpful boost to absorb it much better.

question: When assessing pain using the PQRST mnemonic, what does the letter 'Q' stand for?

options.A: Quiescence
options.B: Quantity
options.C: Quality
options.D: Quickness

explanation: Correct! 'Q' stands for quality—like asking the patient if the pain feels sharp, dull, stabbing, or aching.

question: What should you warn your patient about right before you start a bladder irrigation?

options.A: Immediate drowsiness and heavy sleepiness
options.B: A strong urge to urinate or mild cramping
options.C: Numbness spreading down both upper legs
options.D: A sharp burning sensation in the lower back

explanation: No need to alarm them—just let them know that filling the bladder naturally tricks the body into feeling like it really needs to pee!

question: Why does a sudden dip in blood sugar so quickly lead to confusion and fainting?

options.A: Low sugar causes the brain cells to instantly swell with extra fluid
options.B: The liver stops sending oxygen to the head during sugar crashes
options.C: Nerves stop producing insulin when blood sugar drops below normal
options.D: The brain relies entirely on a continuous supply of circulating glucose

explanation: Unlike other tissues, your brain cells don't store fuel. When blood glucose takes a dive, the brain feels it instantly!

question: Which finding is considered a normal, expected temporary side effect following a cystoscopy procedure?

options.A: Mild burning during urination and slight pink-tinged urine
options.B: Inability to feel the need to urinate for several weeks
options.C: Severe lower abdominal pain radiating to the shoulders
options.D: Complete absence of urine output for twenty-four hours

explanation: Passing the scope through the urethra causes minor irritation and mucosal trauma, leading to temporary burning and light bleeding. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h5)

question: How is a transport monitor different from a simple, pocket-sized pulse oximeter?

options.A: It does not require a power source or battery to function
options.B: It tracks multiple vital parameters simultaneously during critical movement
options.C: It can only measure the patient's body temperature
options.D: It is strictly used for outpatient home care without nursing oversight

explanation: While a pocket oximeter usually only checks oxygen levels, a transport monitor is built to track several vital signs at once during busy or critical moves.

question: A patient complains of severe stomach pain. What does a nurse with strong analytical skills do first?

options.A: Give the strongest pain medication available immediately
options.B: Discharge the patient because pain scales are unreliable
options.C: Tell the patient that stomach pain is normal after surgery
options.D: Check surgical history, lab results, and current medications

explanation: Analytical skills help the nurse look at multiple data sources to understand the root cause before acting. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h3)

question: What complication is a patient most at risk for if they receive many blood transfusions over several years?

options.A: Acute hemolytic shock
options.B: Immediate anaphylaxis
options.C: Bacterial sepsis
options.D: Iron overload

explanation: Our bodies are great at using iron, but terrible at getting rid of excess iron! Over years of multiple transfusions, that extra iron starts piling up in vital organs like the liver and heart.

question: Which group of drugs is most commonly grabbed off the shelf for everyday aches without a prescription?

options.A: Intravenous anesthetics
options.B: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
options.C: Chemotherapy agents
options.D: Injectable insulin products

explanation: That's right! Pain relievers like ibuprofen (NSADs) are easy to buy over the counter, making them hot targets for misuse when body pains flare up.

question: What is the best way to help prevent atelectasis in a patient after surgery?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake to prevent fluid overload in the chest
options.B: Administering a strong sleeping pill to ensure total rest
options.C: Encouraging regular deep breathing and incentive spirometry
options.D: Keeping the patient completely flat in bed to rest the lungs

explanation: Spot on! Getting the patient to take deep breaths and use their incentive spirometer pops those little air sacs wide open and keeps the lungs clear.

question: Why is community diagnosis performed during mobilisation?

options.A: To test every resident for rare genetic disorders
options.B: To collect money from villagers for the clinic roof
options.C: To identify major local health problems and priorities together
options.D: To decide which nurses will be transferred

explanation: Community diagnosis helps health workers and residents discover what health issues matter most to the locals. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h5)

question: A nurse drops a sterile instrument pack on the theatre floor before opening it. What is the correct next step?

options.A: Place the pack back on the shelf for the next procedure
options.B: Open the pack and check if the metal inside looks clean
options.C: Return the pack to the TSSU for complete reprocessing
options.D: Wipe the outside wrapper with alcohol and use it anyway

explanation: You've got this! Once a sterile pack hits the floor, its protective barrier is compromised. You can't trust it anymore—send it back for complete re-sterilization.

question: What is transactional sex?

options.A: Exchanging sexual favors for money, gifts, or basic survival needs
options.B: Participating in formal educational classes about human reproduction
options.C: Signing a legal contract regarding marriage age
options.D: Using mobile banking apps to purchase contraceptive supplies

explanation: Transactional sex occurs when financially vulnerable individuals trade intimacy for economic support, often without using protection. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T9#GNS312_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is the primary goal when treating a patient with anaemia?

options.A: To identify and treat the underlying cause
options.B: To permanently stop all dietary iron intake
options.C: To permanently increase the white blood cell count
options.D: To lower the body temperature to resting levels

explanation: You can't just slap a band-aid on anaemia! Finding out *why* it's happening—whether it's blood loss, heavy periods, or poor nutrition—is key to fixing it.

question: A teenage girl visits the clinic with recurrent chest infections and unusual linear burns across her breasts. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Breast ironing abuse
options.B: A severe allergic skin rash
options.C: Normal adolescent development
options.D: Accidental kitchen scalding

explanation: Unusual burn patterns and repeated infections on the chest during puberty are classic signs of breast ironing. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T17#GNS312_U1_T17_h6)

question: Why must nurses strongly advise patients NEVER to squeeze or pop a vulval cyst at home?

options.A: Squeezing can introduce germs and cause a bad infection
options.B: Manual pressure forces the fluid straight into the bloodstream
options.C: It will instantly trigger cancerous cell growth
options.D: Popping it at home permanently removes the gland

explanation: Trying to pop a cyst at home breaks the delicate skin, lets bacteria in, and can easily turn a painless little cyst into a very painful abscess.

question: Why is angiogenesis so important for a growing malignant tumor?

options.A: It supplies necessary oxygen and nutrients while removing waste
options.B: It prevents the immune system from noticing the tumor mass
options.C: It encapsulates the tumor to keep it from spreading locally
options.D: It repairs damaged DNA inside the fast-growing cancer cells

explanation: You got it! Without a fresh blood supply delivering nutrients and carrying away waste, a tumor would quickly starve and stop growing.

question: Why is giving clear instructions to patients before a screening test so important?

options.A: To reduce the total cost of hospital equipment
options.B: To shorten the time the doctor spends in the clinic
options.C: To stop patients from asking questions about their health
options.D: To ensure the laboratory or screening results are accurate

explanation: Well done! Proper prep prevents wonky readings that could lead to misdiagnosis or unnecessary repeat tests.

question: Why does the baby's head usually rotate internally as it moves down through the pelvis?

options.A: to signal the placenta that it is time to detach from the uterine wall
options.B: to fit the widest part of the head through the widest diameter of the pelvic outlet
options.C: to prevent the umbilical cord from wrapping tightly around the fetal neck
options.D: to decrease the intensity of maternal uterine contractions

explanation: Correct! The pelvis has specific shapes, and the baby rotates to match those contours for a smoother passage through the birth canal.

question: A nurse finishes cleaning and dressing severe chest burns on a young girl rescued from breast ironing. What is the next essential step in her holistic care?

options.A: Discharging the patient home with basic oral antibiotics
options.B: Involving child protection and mental health services
options.C: Telling the mother to return only if new blisters appear
options.D: Scheduling a follow-up appointment in six months

explanation: Ensuring the child's immediate physical and emotional safety through protection agencies and counseling is a top priority. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T17#GNS312_U1_T17_h7)

question: What piece of info is automatically attached to every single entry you make in an EMR?

options.A: The brand name of the computer monitor used
options.B: The patient's bank account and credit score
options.C: The user login ID, date, and exact timestamp
options.D: The GPS coordinates of the hospital building

explanation: Digital charts automatically stamp your notes with metadata, proving precisely who entered the information and when.

question: What visual characteristic does urine often have in a patient with nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: Dark red and bloody
options.B: Frothy or foamy appearance
options.C: Thick and milky white
options.D: Bright neon green color

explanation: The large amount of protein spilling into the urine changes its surface tension, creating a noticeable frothy or foamy look when the patient voids. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h3)

question: What is the main goal of primary prevention in haematology?

options.A: To manage chronic pain in sickle cell disease
options.B: To detect early signs of a bleeding disorder
options.C: To stop a blood disorder from ever developing
options.D: To cure a patient with advanced leukemia

explanation: Primary prevention focuses on stopping diseases before they start through healthy lifestyle habits and vaccinations. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h1)

question: What is one of the biggest reasons operating room nurses experience mental burnout?

options.A: Having too many tea breaks during a single shift
options.B: Having zero paperwork or chart writing to do
options.C: The constant pressure and need to watch life-and-death details
options.D: Spending too many hours relaxing at a computer desk

explanation: Staying fully alert and focused during critical surgeries drains your emotional and mental energy. It is totally normal to feel tired, so self-care is vital!

question: Why does chronic high blood pressure cause small arteries to permanently narrow over time?

options.A: The heart pumps less blood, causing arteries to shrink from lack of use
options.B: Smooth muscle in the vessel walls thickens in response to the pressure
options.C: Blood clots constantly form and dissolve inside the walls
options.D: Red blood cells stick together and clog the tiny vessels

explanation: Constant high pressure forces the tiny muscles in artery walls to bulk up and thicken, which leaves less open space inside for blood to flow through.

question: Which post-procedure symptom should a patient report to the healthcare provider immediately?

options.A: A mild chalky taste remaining in the mouth briefly
options.B: Passing pale white stools for the first 24 hours
options.C: Feeling slightly tired after changing positions on the table
options.D: Severe abdominal pain and inability to pass gas

explanation: Severe abdominal pain and lack of gas or stool suggest a bowel obstruction from hardened barium, which requires urgent medical attention. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T13#GNS221_U2_T13_h8)

question: What kind of bowel sounds do you usually hear early on when a patient has a mechanical small bowel obstruction?

options.A: Completely absent sounds
options.B: Normal regular gurgles
options.C: Sustained swishing bruits
options.D: High-pitched, tinkling sounds

explanation: As the bowel strains to push contents past the tight spot, it creates those characteristic high-pitched, tinkling sounds right above the blockage.

question: What triggers a homeostatic imbalance in the human body?

options.A: When a person sleeps for more than eight hours
options.B: When disease or trauma overwhelms normal control systems
options.C: When vital signs stay completely stable for a long time
options.D: When the body eats a balanced diet with fresh fruits

explanation: Well done! When illness or injury hits hard, it can strain or break the natural feedback loops that keep the body balanced.

question: What should you do immediately if mixed medications inside a syringe driver turn cloudy?

options.A: Vigorously shake the syringe to dissolve the cloudy particles back in
options.B: Leave the pump running because color changes are completely normal
options.C: Increase the infusion rate to push the cloudy solution through faster
options.D: Discard the mixture immediately because the drugs are likely incompatible

explanation: Well done! Cloudiness means a chemical reaction happened between the drugs, making them unsafe. Never give a cloudy mixture—always prepare a fresh, safe set.

question: Why are teenagers more likely to take risks than adults?

options.A: The emotional limbic system matures faster than the impulse-controlling prefrontal cortex
options.B: The brain stops producing neurotransmitters entirely during puberty
options.C: The adolescent brain requires less sleep than the adult brain
options.D: Synaptic pruning causes a temporary loss of all memory function

explanation: You got it! The brain's emotional center develops faster than the part that controls impulses, making teens more prone to seeking thrills.

question: Why might a patient with a weak immune system who has a severe infection not show typical pus or swelling?

options.A: Their skin is too tough for localized swelling to become visible
options.B: Their body temperature is always too low to allow fluid accumulation
options.C: Their circulatory system moves blood too fast for fluid to leak
options.D: They lack an adequate number of white blood cells to create an inflammatory response

explanation: You're doing great! Pus and swelling are signs that white blood cells are fighting hard. If a patient doesn't have enough white blood cells, that visible battle scene won't show up.

question: A patient with advanced lung cancer takes chemotherapy to shrink a tumor and also takes medicine for breathlessness and pain. What type of care is this?

options.A: Purely experimental care with no proven benefit
options.B: Curative care only, because pain is a minor symptom
options.C: A combination of curative and palliative care
options.D: Palliative care only, because chemotherapy has stopped

explanation: This is a great combo! The chemo fights the cancer (curative), while the pain meds keep the patient comfortable (palliative). They work wonderfully together.

question: What is the very first thing a nurse should check before moving a patient to a chair?

options.A: The color of the patient's room walls
options.B: The brand name of the hospital bed
options.C: The patient's current ability to bear weight
options.D: The exact time the doctor's shift ends

explanation: Always check if the patient can stand or support themselves first! This tells you if you need an extra pair of hands or a mechanical lift.

question: What is the primary purpose of using the topical route of administration?

options.A: To guarantee immediate intravenous bloodstream entry
options.B: To force rapid first-pass liver metabolism of the drug
options.C: To treat a local condition directly on a body surface
options.D: To bypass the need for any skin or mucous membrane contact

explanation: Topical medications are primarily applied directly to the skin or mucous membranes to treat surface-level issues right where they are placed. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h1)

question: Why should a patient with uncontrolled epilepsy wear a medical alert bracelet?

options.A: To prove to the police that they can drive a car
options.B: To track how many hours of sleep they get each night
options.C: To store extra doses of anti-seizure medication
options.D: To ensure bystanders and emergency workers know what is wrong

explanation: If a patient can't speak for themselves after a fit, that little bracelet does the talking for them, making sure helpers know exactly what condition they have.

question: What does the term 'white-coat syndrome' mean in a hospital setting?

options.A: A skin rash caused by wearing polyester clinic uniforms
options.B: Extreme fear of surgical instruments and needles
options.C: Temporary high blood pressure caused by anxiety about seeing a nurse or doctor
options.D: An allergic reaction to latex examination gloves

explanation: Spot on! The clinic environment can make anyone nervous, causing a temporary spike in blood pressure readings.

question: A patient arrives sweating heavily with thick makeup on their forehead. What should you do for their temperature?

options.A: Use the temporal thermometer right over the makeup
options.B: Use another route, like the ear or mouth
options.C: Wipe the forehead with alcohol and read immediately
options.D: Add two degrees to whatever the temporal reading says

explanation: Sweat and cosmetics mess up forehead heat readings. Save yourself a headache and switch to an oral or tympanic route!

question: What is a very common feeling for someone newly admitted to a hospital?

options.A: Complete emotional indifference to surroundings
options.B: Anxiety and a sense of vulnerability
options.C: Total independence over institutional schedules
options.D: Overwhelming joy regarding hospital routines

question: Why can frequent exposure to high scrotal heat, like hot baths or saunas, lower a man's fertility?

options.A: It interferes with normal sperm production and development
options.B: It destroys the prostate gland and seminal vesicles
options.C: It blocks the release of testosterone from the adrenal glands
options.D: It causes permanent scarring of the vas deferens tubes

explanation: Fantastic! Sperm need a cozy spot slightly cooler than normal body temperature to grow properly, so extra heat disrupts the whole process.

question: What is the single most common trigger for Acute Glomerulonephritis globally and in Nigeria?

options.A: Streptococcal infection
options.B: Direct kidney trauma
options.C: A severe snake bite
options.D: High dietary salt intake

question: Why is active listening and counseling so important when nursing patients with reproductive issues?

options.A: To make sure they follow hospital visiting hours
options.B: To diagnose mental health disorders on our own
options.C: To replace the need for any surgery or medicine
options.D: To help them talk through emotional pain and body worries

explanation: Wonderful! Reproductive issues can bring deep worry and sadness. Listening to our patients validates their feelings and supports total healing.

question: How can you best support a patient who is experiencing deep emotional distress and fear?

options.A: Change the subject immediately to something cheerful
options.B: Limit family visits to reduce emotional conversations
options.C: Tell the patient not to worry because everything happens for a reason
options.D: Listen actively and validate the patient's difficult feelings

explanation: Active listening and validation make patients feel seen and heard, proving that their emotional pain matters just as much as physical symptoms. You're becoming a wonderful nurse!

question: What is an embolus?

options.A: A traveling blood clot or foreign object moving through the bloodstream
options.B: An infection of the outer heart lining
options.C: A normal hole between the right and left atrium
options.D: A sudden widening of the aorta

explanation: An embolus is basically a traveler you don't want! It's any loose mass floating through the blood vessels until it gets stuck in a smaller vessel and blocks the path.

question: Why must a patient take a special bowel cleaning solution before having a colonoscopy?

options.A: To clear all stool so the doctor can see the lining clearly
options.B: To numb the inside of the rectum before the scope goes in
options.C: To relax the abdominal muscles and prevent cramping
options.D: To kill harmful bacteria living in the sigmoid colon

explanation: Exactly right! Any leftover stool blocks the camera view and can hide small polyps or early trouble spots, so a completely clean bowel is a must.

question: Why is the symptothermal method (using multiple signs together) more reliable than just watching one sign?

options.A: It forces the ovaries to release eggs on a strict schedule
options.B: It prevents hormonal fluctuations from happening during the cycle
options.C: It eliminates the need to record daily observations on a chart
options.D: Cross-checking multiple body signs reduces the chance of misinterpreting the fertile window

explanation: Two checks are better than one! Combining temperature and mucus signs gives a much clearer picture of your fertile days.
